newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss private banking assets top $1.8 trillion.
newsitem.headline: Swiss private banking assets top $1.8 trillion.

text.p: Switzerland remains at the top of the world's private banking league with estimated assets of $1.8 trillion under management, but tough competition is putting pressure on margins and growth, a new study said on Friday.

Almost all banks are expanding the lucrative business of private asset management which grew 13 percent on average a year in 1990-1995 with commission income up 11 percent annually, the study published by Credit Suisse First Boston Bank (CSFB) said.
The study said Swiss asset management firms should continue to grow, albeit slightly slower than their global rivals which expect to grow by 10-20 percent a year in the next five years.
Annual growth at Swiss private banking business should slow down to 10 percent for assets and eight percent for commissions in the coming years amid growing competition, it added.

"Virtually all banks intend to expand the asset management business, whose attractions lie in its growth potential, stability, profitability and equity financing," said Madeleine Hoffmann, author of the study.
"Margins are thus almost certain to remain under pressure. We expect that tougher competition will cause a more modest pace of growth," said Hoffmann.

The study said Switzerland held 35-45 percent of the global private wealth business, followed by London and U.S. centres with 15 percent each, Hong Kong and Singapore 10 percent and Luxembourg, Channel Islands and other centres 5-10 percent each.
Growing competition with the arrival of such Wall Street powerhouses as Merrill Lynch and JP Morgan has brought whirlwind changes to the once-cozy world of Swiss private bankers.
Competition is forcing some private banks to expand aggressively into emerging markets to tap new riches overseas.
Almost all major retail banks now provide private banking services to the rich, joining old, established private banks offering traditional red-carpet services.
Pierre Poncet, managing partner at Bordier & Cie, one of Geneva's oldest private banks founded in 1844, estimated that liquid wealth in Switzerland grew by 25 percent in 1996.
He estimated that performance contributed up to 20 percent to the growth in the industry and new clients another five to 10 percent in 1996, when market rallies provided good returns.
In 1997, performance growth should slow down to between seven and 12 percent, he added.

"Competition is a fact of life, but it has stabilised," Poncet told Reuters. "Private banking is a big growth area. New markets are opening up, new instruments are emerging and new wealth is being created."

The CSFB study said Swiss private banks were no longer demanding excessively high fees. "In terms of overall costs, Swiss banks today can easily hold their own against centres such as London, New York, Paris and Frankfurt," it said.
Commissions were 0.52 percent of assets at Bank Julius Baer, 0.73 percent at LGT Bank and 0.49 percent at Gotthard Bank.

The study said that leading Swiss asset management institutions quoted on the Zurich bourse such as Bank Julius Baer, VP Bank, LGT and Gotthard Bank offered good returns for longer-term investors. Earnings per share were growing by 14.7 percent a year on average at Julius baer, 25.3 percent at LGT and 13.1 percent at VP Bank.
